title: Plate Tectonics and the Age of the Crust
seo_title: Plate Tectonics Worksheets: Seafloor Spreading, Crust Ages and Boundaries (Earth Science)
standard_text: Evaluate evidence of the past and current movements of continental and oceanic crust and the theory of plate tectonics to explain the ages of crustal rocks.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on plate tectonics (NGSS HS-ESS1-5): seafloor spreading rates, crust ages, magnetic stripes, plate boundaries and evidence for drift. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Seafloor is young; continents are old.
key_sub: New crust forms at ridges and is recycled at trenches; light continental crust stays.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plates move, so crust is made, moved and recycled.

  • New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and gets older with distance. Spreading rate = distance ÷ age.
  • Oceanic crust sinks at subduction zones, so it is never older than about 180 million years. Light continental crust stays, so it can be billions of years old.
  • Evidence: matching fossils and rocks, magnetic stripes, seafloor ages and GPS.
Example

Rock 500 km from the ridge is 20 million years old. Rate?

5 × 107 cm ÷ 2 × 107 yr

Answer: 2.5 cm per year

Example

Where is the oldest seafloor?

Farthest from the ridge

Answer: near trenches and continental edges

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the oldest seafloor is at the ridge.
  • Thinking oceanic crust is as old as Earth.
  • Thinking plates move meters per year.

faq.q: Why is seafloor younger than continents?
faq.a: Oceanic crust forms at ridges and sinks back into the mantle at subduction zones within about 200 million years, but light continental crust is not subducted.

faq.q: How do you find a seafloor spreading rate?
faq.a: Divide the distance from the ridge by the age of the rock, converting km to cm and million years to years.

faq.q: What is the evidence for plate tectonics?
faq.a: Matching fossils and rocks across oceans, symmetric magnetic stripes, seafloor ages that increase away from ridges, and GPS measurements of moving plates.

items.q: What is subduction?
c: one plate sinking beneath another into the mantle

items.q: Which evidence best supports this idea: “The rocks formed together before the continents split.”
c: Glacier scratches in India and Africa point in directions that only make sense if the continents were joined.
Rock layers and mountain belts match across the Atlantic Ocean.
The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.
The same fossil reptile, Mesosaurus, is found in South America and Africa.

items.q: Evidence: GPS stations show Hawaii moving about 7 cm per year toward Japan. What does it support?
c: The rocks formed together before the continents split.
The continents may once have been joined.
The southern continents were together near the South Pole.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
c: a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow

items.q: Two continental plates collide, as India hit Asia. What feature forms?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanic mountains
a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
very high folded mountains like the Himalayas
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

items.q: An ocean plate sinks under a continent, as off South America. What feature forms?
c: very high folded mountains like the Himalayas
a trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands
a deep trench and a chain of volcanic mountains
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

Why can continental rocks be up to 4 billion years old?
c: Continental crust is thick and light, so it does not sink back into the mantle.
